articles.name: Using suggested assignees to reassign tickets
articles.title: Using suggested assignees to reassign tickets
articles.body:
Suggested assignees help you identify the best agent to handle a ticket when it needs to be reassigned or escalated. Based on historical ticket data, Zendesk recommends agents who have resolved similar issues and shows a confidence level for each recommendation. You can review the suggested agents and related resolved tickets, then reassign the ticket in one click.

What's my plan?
Add-on Copilot

Summary: ◀▼

Use suggested assignees to reassign or escalate tickets to agents with experience resolving similar issues. Review each agent’s confidence level, group, and related resolved tickets to choose the right person, then assign the ticket in one click. You can limit suggestions to the ticket’s group or use standard assignment options instead. Suggested assignees complement omnichannel routing for later ticket changes.

Suggested assignees help you identify the best agent to handle a ticket when it needs to be reassigned or escalated. Based on historical ticket data, Zendesk recommends agents who have resolved similar issues and shows a confidence level for each recommendation. You can review the suggested agents and related resolved tickets, then reassign the ticket in one click.

Related articles:
  • Turning on suggested assignees

Reassigning tickets to suggested assignees

When reassigning or escalating a ticket, you can see suggested assignee recommendations in the ticket interface to help you route the ticket to the right agent.

Note: Omnichannel routing (OCR) and suggested assignees can be used together. While OCR is used for the initial routing of new and unassigned tickets, suggested assignees helps you choose an assignee when you need to reassign a ticket or escalate a complex issue later in the workflow.

To reassign tickets to suggested assignees

  1. Open a ticket.
  2. Click the Assignee field to open the reassignment interface.

    Suggested agents' groups appear below their names.

  3. Click View all suggested assignees.
  4. Review the list of suggested assignees. Each suggestion includes:
    • The agent, their email, and their group
    • A confidence level indicating how well-suited they are for this ticket
    • Context about similar tickets they've handled

  5. (Optional) To view agents only in the same group as the ticket, deselect Include agents from other groups.

    Agents from other groups are included by default.

  6. (Optional) Click a similar resolved ticket to open it in a new window.
  7. Click Assign next to your chosen agent to reassign the ticket.

If you prefer to assign manually, continue using the standard assignment options below the suggestions list.

Article Q&A

Click to view

How do I reassign a ticket to a suggested assignee?

Open the ticket, click the Assignee field, and select View all suggested assignees. Review the recommendations and click Assign next to the agent you choose. You can also use the standard assignment options below the suggestions to assign manually.

What information can I use to choose a suggested assignee, and can I limit suggestions to my ticket’s group?

Each suggestion shows the agent’s name, email, group, confidence level, and context about similar tickets they’ve handled. Agents from other groups are included by default; deselect Include agents from other groups to show only agents in the same group as the ticket. You can click a similar resolved ticket to open it in a new window.

Can I use suggested assignees with Omnichannel routing?

Yes. Omnichannel routing handles the initial routing of new and unassigned tickets, while suggested assignees helps you choose an agent when reassigning a ticket or escalating a complex issue later in the workflow.

articles.name: Migrating from the Talk SDK to the Messaging SDK
articles.title: Migrating from the Talk SDK to the Messaging SDK
articles.body:
This guide explains how to migrate your mobile application from the Zendesk Talk SDK to the Zendesk Messaging SDK.

What's my plan?
All Suites Professional, Enterprise, or Enterprise Plus
Support with Talk Professional or Enterprise

This guide explains how to migrate your mobile application from the Zendesk Talk SDK to the Zendesk Messaging SDK.

The migration applies to Android and iOS applications. It requires changes to your mobile application, followed by a new build and release through the relevant app store.

Before you begin, review the SDK removal announcement and the migration deadline of October 15, 2027.

This guide includes the following topics:

  • Understanding and preparing for the migration
  • Migrating from the Talk SDK to the Messaging SDK
  • Testing the migration in a sandbox environment
  • Rolling back the migration
  • Releasing the migrated application
  • Need help?

Understanding and preparing for the migration

This topic includes the following sections:

  • Key differences between the Talk SDK and Messaging SDK
  • Known limitations
  • Preparing for the migration
  • Migration readiness checklist

Key differences between the Talk SDK and Messaging SDK

The Talk SDK and Messaging SDK use different backend services and provide different experiences. This is not a data migration between the two SDKs.

The Messaging SDK provides in-app messaging and automated support. It does not provide native voice calling or an embedded calling experience equivalent to the Talk SDK.

The following items do not automatically transfer:

  • Talk SDK voice configuration and digital-line setup
  • Talk SDK call history and voice interactions in the mobile experience
  • Talk SDK call controls and call-screen behavior
  • Talk SDK identities and authentication configuration
  • Talk SDK configuration and UI customizations

End users start with a new Messaging state and will not see previous Talk interactions in the Messaging SDK. Review any data-retention, export, or compliance requirements with your Zendesk account team before the Talk service ends.

Choose one of the following voice paths:

  • Zendesk Voice: use the Messaging SDK for in-app support and provide voice through a separate Zendesk phone channel. Calls no longer start inside the app.
  • SIP-IN: if your organization already uses SIP-IN, retain the existing integration for voice while adopting the Messaging SDK for in-app support. Confirm that the integration and commercial arrangements remain available for your account.
  • No voice channel: use the Messaging SDK for in-app messaging and automated support only.

Known limitations

  • The Messaging SDK does not provide native voice calling or an embedded in-app calling experience equivalent to the Talk SDK.
  • Zendesk Voice provides a separate phone channel; calls no longer start inside the mobile application.
  • SIP-IN can be retained only for customers that already have an existing SIP-IN integration and the integration remains available for their account.
  • Talk voice history, configuration, and customizations do not transfer to the Messaging SDK.
  • End users start with a blank Messaging state and cannot access previous Talk interactions through the Messaging SDK.
  • A rollback cannot expose Messaging conversations through the Talk SDK.
  • If the Talk backend is shut down, Talk SDK initialization will fail.

Preparing for the migration

Before starting the migration, make sure that:

  • You have access to Admin Center.
  • You can create or configure a messaging channel.
  • You have access to your mobile application source code and build environment.
  • A mobile developer and Zendesk administrator are available.
  • You have a non-production Zendesk account or dedicated sandbox channel.
  • You have reviewed the Messaging SDK documentation for your platform.
  • You have decided whether your future voice path will be Zendesk Voice, an existing SIP-IN integration, or no voice channel.

Complete the required account-side setup before releasing the updated mobile application.

Migration readiness checklist

Before beginning production migration, confirm that:

  • The Talk SDK end-of-life announcement and migration deadline have been reviewed.
  • The required Messaging channel is configured.
  • Your Zendesk Voice or SIP-IN path is confirmed, if voice remains required.
  • The supported Android or iOS SDK version is confirmed.
  • Sandbox testing has succeeded.
  • You have a staged rollout or rollback plan.
  • You understand that Talk voice history and configuration will not transfer.
  • You have reviewed any data-retention, export, or compliance requirements.

Migrating from the Talk SDK to the Messaging SDK

This topic includes the following tasks:

  • Step 1: Creating a messaging channel
  • Step 2: Confirming your voice path
  • Step 3: Adding the Messaging SDK
  • Step 4: Removing Talk SDK initialization
  • Step 5: Initializing the Messaging SDK
  • Step 6: Configuring end-user authentication
  • Step 7: Replacing Talk SDK screens
  • Step 8: Configuring push notifications
  • Step 9: Building and resolving errors

Step 1: Creating a Messaging channel

  1. In Admin Center, click Channels in the sidebar, then select Messaging and social > Messaging.
  2. Create or identify the messaging channel that your mobile application will use.
  3. Obtain the channel key and provide it to your mobile developer.
  4. Use a separate messaging channel for sandbox testing where possible.

Step 2: Confirming your voice path

  1. Decide whether the application will use Zendesk Voice, retain an existing SIP-IN integration, or stop offering voice in the mobile application.
  2. If you use Zendesk Voice, configure the phone channel and plan where the Call us entry point will appear in the application. If you use SIP-IN, confirm the existing integration remains available before removing the Talk SDK.

Step 3: Adding the Messaging SDK

  1. Add the supported Messaging SDK package for Android, iOS, or both platforms according to the platform-specific installation instructions.
  2. Remove the Talk SDK package and any dependencies that are used only by the Talk SDK.

Step 4: Removing Talk SDK initialization

Remove Talk SDK initialization, digital-line setup, call initiation code, call controls, call-screen entry points, and any Talk-specific configuration or identity code that is no longer required.

Step 5: Initializing the Messaging SDK

Initialize the Messaging SDK early in your application lifecycle. Handle initialization failure explicitly so that your application can present an appropriate fallback if initialization does not succeed.

Step 6: Configuring end-user authentication

Configure authentication for the Messaging SDK using the supported Messaging authentication flow. Talk SDK authentication is not compatible with the Messaging backend.

If Talk SDK and Messaging SDK are temporarily present in the same application version, caller identification may appear as Unknown Caller and metadata may not pass to the Talk SDK.

Step 7: Replacing Talk SDK screens

  1. Replace Talk SDK entry points with the messaging conversation experience.
  2. Remove the Talk call button and call screen from the application unless you are retaining a separate, approved voice integration such as SIP-IN or a Zendesk Voice phone entry point.

Step 8: Configuring push notifications

  1. Configure push notifications for the Messaging SDK according to the Android and iOS documentation.
  2. Do not reuse Talk-specific notification or configuration assumptions.
  3. Verify that a background message produces a notification and that selecting it opens the correct conversation.

Step 9: Building and resolving errors

  1. Update imports and dependencies, remove dead Talk SDK code, and resolve build errors caused by the package and initialization changes.
  2. Confirm that the application builds successfully without unresolved Talk SDK dependencies.

Testing the migration in a sandbox environment

Test in a non-production Zendesk account using a dedicated messaging channel key. Before releasing the migrated application, verify:

  • The application builds successfully on each supported platform.
  • The Messaging SDK initializes successfully and handles initialization failure gracefully.
  • The messaging entry point opens the conversation experience.
  • A message appears in Agent Workspace and new conversations can be created.
  • Authentication associates the conversation with the expected user, if authentication is used.
  • Push notifications work on supported Android and iOS versions.
  • The Zendesk Voice phone path works, if selected.
  • The existing SIP-IN voice path remains available, if selected.

Rolling back the migration

The Talk SDK and Messaging SDK use separate backends. If you need to roll back before the migrated application is fully released:

  • Revert the dependency changes.
  • Restore Talk SDK initialization and configuration.
  • Restore Talk SDK identity configuration and UI entry points.
  • Restore the required Talk SDK notification configuration.
  • Rebuild and reinstall the application.

A rollback does not make Messaging conversations visible through the Talk SDK. Conversations created through messaging remain associated with the messaging channel and are not synchronized with the Talk backend. Use staged rollout, feature flags, or an A/B testing mechanism where available to reduce deployment risk.

Releasing the migrated application

After sandbox testing is complete:

  • Complete the required Zendesk account-side setup.
  • Confirm that the selected voice path is ready for production, if applicable.
  • Merge the mobile code changes and build the production application.
  • Submit the application to the relevant app store.
  • Use a staged rollout where available.
  • Monitor initialization, authentication, messaging, push notifications, voice entry points, and crash reports.
  • After the migrated version is available, remove the Talk SDK from the production build.

Older app versions may continue to exist after the new version is released. The migration is complete only when affected end users have installed an application version that uses the Messaging SDK and the Talk SDK is no longer required for the supported experience.

Need help?

Review the Messaging SDK documentation and this migration guide.

For account-specific questions about Zendesk Voice, SIP-IN availability, data retention, or your Talk retirement date, contact your Zendesk account team or submit a support request through the standard Zendesk Support process.

articles.name: Migrating from the Support SDK to the Messaging SDK for Android and iOS
articles.title: Migrating from the Support SDK to the Messaging SDK for Android and iOS
articles.body:
This guide explains how to migrate your mobile application from the Zendesk Support SDK to the Zendesk Messaging SDK on Android and iOS. Migration requires changes to your mobile application, followed by a new build and release through the relevant app store.

This guide explains how to migrate your mobile application from the Zendesk Support SDK to the Zendesk Messaging SDK on Android and iOS. Migration requires changes to your mobile application, followed by a new build and release through the relevant app store.

Before you begin, review the SDK removal announcement and the migration deadline of October 15, 2027.

This guide includes the following topics:

  • Understanding and preparing for the migration
  • Migrating from the Support SDK for Android to the Messaging SDK
  • Migrating from the Support SDK for iOS to the Messaging SDK
  • Testing the migration in a sandbox environment
  • Rolling back the migration
  • Releasing the migration
  • Need help?

Understanding the migration

This topic includes the following sections:

  • Key differences between the Support SDK and Messaging SDK
  • Known limitations
  • Preparing for the migration
  • Migration readiness checklist

Key differences between the Support SDKs and Messaging SDK

The Support SDK and Messaging SDK use different backend services and provide different experiences. Migrating the SDK changes the mobile experience and backend integration; it does not migrate existing conversations, ticket history, or other data into the Messaging SDK.

The following items do not automatically transfer:

  • Existing Support SDK conversations
  • Legacy chat sessions
  • Ticket history shown in the Support SDK
  • Support SDK identities
  • Support SDK configuration and UI customizations

Authenticated users may be associated with an existing Zendesk user when the Messaging JWT contains the appropriate identity information and authentication is configured correctly.

Previous conversations and ticket history will not appear in the Messaging SDK conversation list. Agents may still be able to access existing tickets in Agent Workspace, depending on your Zendesk configuration.

The Messaging SDK provides a conversational experience. If your application uses Support SDK Guide, decide whether users need conversational article answers or a standalone Help Center experience. An AI agent can surface relevant articles in the conversation, but this does not replace Help Center browsing, search, category navigation, or direct access to restricted articles. Ticket forms and custom fields may also require an alternative messaging implementation.

Known limitations

  • Existing Support SDK conversations and ticket history do not transfer to the Messaging SDK experience.
  • Support SDK identities are not automatically carried over.
  • The Messaging SDK does not provide a standalone native Guide browsing and search experience equivalent to the Support SDK. Use conversational article answers or a Help Center webview or external browser as the interim replacement.
  • Ticket forms and custom fields may require an alternative messaging implementation.
  • The Messaging SDK is not aware of the full ticket lifecycle in Agent Workspace.
  • Push notifications cover messaging conversation updates, not all ticket-level updates.
  • A rollback cannot expose messaging conversations through the Support SDK.
  • Zendesk will provide advance notice before any Support SDK backend services are retired.

Preparing for the migration

Before starting the migration, make sure that:

  • You have access to Admin Center.
  • You can create or configure a messaging channel.
  • You have access to your mobile application source code and build environment.
  • A mobile developer and Zendesk administrator are available.
  • You have a non-production Zendesk account or dedicated sandbox channel.
  • You have reviewed the Messaging SDK documentation for your platform.
  • The messaging features and approved replacements required by your application are available for your platform.
  • You inventory the Support SDK features used by your application before you begin. Include authentication, Help Center or Guide, ticket forms, custom fields, attachments, push notifications, request history, and deep links.

Complete the required account-side migration before releasing the updated mobile application.

Migration readiness checklist

Before beginning production migration, confirm that:

  • The required account-side migration is complete or scheduled.
  • The required messaging capabilities are available for your target platform.
  • Your forms, Guide or Help Center, article, authentication, attachment, and push use cases have an approved replacement.
  • The supported Android or iOS SDK version is confirmed.
  • Sandbox testing has succeeded.
  • You have a staged rollout or rollback plan.
  • You understand that legacy in-app history will not transfer.

Migrating to the Messaging SDK for Android

This topic includes the following tasks:

  • Step 1: Creating a messaging channel
  • Step 2: Checking platform requirements
  • Step 3: Adding the Messaging SDK
  • Step 4: Removing Support SDK initialization
  • Step 5: Initializing the Messaging SDK
  • Step 6: Configuring end-user authentication
  • Step 7: Replacing Support SDK screens
  • Step 8: Reconfiguring push notifications
  • Step 9: Cleaning up ProGuard and R8 rules
  • Step 10: Resolving build errors

Step 1: Creating a Messaging channel

  1. In Admin Center, create or identify the messaging channel that your mobile application will use.
  2. Obtain the channel key. The channel key replaces the following Support SDK configuration values:
    • zendeskUrl
    • applicationId
    • oauthClientId
  3. Use a separate messaging channel for sandbox testing where possible.

Step 2: Checking your platform requirements

  1. Confirm that your project meets the requirements for the Messaging SDK version you are adopting. The current engineering reference application uses:
    • minSdk = 24
    • compileSdk = 37
    • Java 17
    • Kotlin 2.3.x
  2. These requirements may change. Confirm the requirements for the supported SDK version before starting your migration.

Step 3: Adding the Messaging SDK

  1. Add the public Zendesk Maven repository if it is not already configured: 
    dependencyResolutionManagement {
    repositoriesMode.set(RepositoriesMode.FAIL_ON_PROJECT_REPOS)

    repositories {
        google()
        mavenCentral()
        maven {
            url = uri("https://zendesk.jfrog.io/artifactory/repo")
        }
    }
}
  2. Remove the Support SDK: 
    implementation("com.zendesk:support:5.x")
  3. Also remove related Support SDK dependencies, such as: 
    com.zendesk:guide
com.zendesk:support-providers
com.zendesk:sdk-configurations
  4. Add the supported Messaging SDK version: 
    implementation("zendesk.messaging:messaging-android:[supported version]")

Step 4: Removing Support SDK initialization

  1. Remove Support SDK initialization code, including: 
    Zendesk.INSTANCE.init(...)
Support.INSTANCE.init(...)
AnswerBot.INSTANCE.init(...)
Zendesk.INSTANCE.setIdentity(...)
  2. Remove any associated configuration and identity code that is no longer required.

Step 5: Initializing the Messaging SDK

  • Initialize the Messaging SDK early in your application lifecycle: 
    import zendesk.android.Zendesk
import zendesk.messaging.android.DefaultMessagingFactory

override fun onCreate() {
    super.onCreate()

    Zendesk.initialize(
        this,
        getString(R.string.channel_key),
        successCallback = { zendesk ->
            // Initialization succeeded.
        },
        failureCallback = { error ->
            // Initialization failed.
            // Execute your application fallback.
        },
        messagingFactory = DefaultMessagingFactory()
    )
}

Your application should handle initialization failure explicitly.

Step 6: Configuring end-user authentication

Support SDK identities are not automatically transferred to the Messaging SDK.

  1. If your application authenticates end users, configure the supported messaging authentication flow using a Sunshine Conversations JWT. This remains required when users need access to restricted Help Center articles. The conversation-extension getContext token is a separate webview-to-backend authentication mechanism. 
    import zendesk.android.ZendeskAuthenticationDelegate

Zendesk.authenticationDelegate =
    ZendeskAuthenticationDelegate { _, updateToken ->
        // Fetch a fresh JWT from your backend.
        updateToken(jwt)
    }
  2. Log in an authenticated user: 
    Zendesk.instance.loginUser(
    jwt,
    successCallback = { user ->
        // User authentication succeeded.
    },
    failureCallback = { error ->
        // Handle authentication failure.
    }
)
  3. Log out a user when required: 
    Zendesk.instance.logoutUser(
    successCallback = {
        // User logged out.
    },
    failureCallback = { error ->
        // Handle logout failure.
    }
)
  4. Make sure your backend can issue and refresh the required JWTs before releasing the migrated application.

Step 7: Replacing Support SDK screens

  1. Replace Support SDK UI entry points with the messaging conversation experience. 
    import zendesk.android.Zendesk

Zendesk.instance.messaging.showMessaging(this)
  2. Remove references to:
    • RequestActivity
    • RequestListActivity
    • HelpCenterActivity
    • ViewArticleActivity
    • Answer Bot entry points
Note: Before removing these entry points, confirm the approved replacement for each workflow. An AI agent can provide conversational article answers, but it does not replace standalone Help Center browsing and search. Use a Help Center webview or external browser for that workflow, and validate messaging JWT authentication if restricted articles are required.

Step 8: Reconfiguring push notifications

The Support SDK push notification implementation does not apply to the Messaging SDK.

Do not reuse Support-specific Firebase services or configuration providers.

Follow the Messaging SDK push notification documentation to:

  • Register the device token with Zendesk.
  • Configure Firebase Cloud Messaging for Android.
  • Verify that a background message produces a notification.
  • Verify that selecting the notification opens the correct conversation.

Step 9: Clean up ProGuard and R8 rules

The Messaging SDK includes its consumer rules automatically.

  1. Remove obsolete Support SDK rules, such as: 
    -keepclassmembers class zendesk.support.** { *; }
-keep class zendesk.support.request.** { *; }
-keep class zendesk.support.requestlist.** { *; }
-keep class zendesk.support.request.ViewCellAttachmentMenuItem { *; }
  2. Review your project for other custom rules that reference removed Support SDK packages.

Step 10: Resolve build errors

  1. Update imports from the Support SDK package names to the Messaging SDK package names.

    The package roots change from:

    com.zendesk.*
zendesk.support.*

    to:

    zendesk.android.*
zendesk.messaging.android.*
  2. Remove dead Support SDK code instead of leaving unused code or temporary stubs.

Migrating to the Messaging SDK for iOS

This topic includes the following tasks:

  • Step 1: Creating a messaging channel
  • Step 2: Checking platform requirements
  • Step 3: Adding the Messaging SDK
  • Step 4: Removing Support SDK initialization
  • Step 5: Initializing the Messaging SDK
  • Step 6: Configuring end-user authentication
  • Step 7: Replacing Support SDK screens
  • Step 8: Reconfiguring push notifications
  • Step 9: Cleaning up ProGuard and R8 rules
  • Step 10: Resolving build errors

Step 1: Creating a Messaging channel

  1. In Admin Center, create or identify the messaging channel that your mobile application will use.
  2. Obtain the channel key. The channel key replaces the following Support SDK configuration values:
    • zendeskUrl
    • applicationId
    • oauthClientId
  3. Use a separate messaging channel for sandbox testing where possible.

Step 2: Checking your platform requirements

Follow the supported platform and deployment-target requirements in the Messaging SDK for iOS documentation.

Step 3: Adding the Messaging SDK

Remove the Support SDK package and add the supported Messaging SDK package according to the iOS installation instructions.

Step 4: Removing Support SDK initialization

  1. Remove Support SDK initialization code, including: 
    Zendesk.INSTANCE.init(...)
Support.INSTANCE.init(...)
AnswerBot.INSTANCE.init(...)
Zendesk.INSTANCE.setIdentity(...)
  2. Remove any associated configuration and identity code that is no longer required.

Step 5: Initializing the Messaging SDK

Initialize the Messaging SDK early in your application lifecycle.

Import the SDK modules:

import ZendeskSDK
import ZendeskSDKMessaging

If your app uses authenticated users or restricted Help Center articles, configure the authentication delegate before initializing the SDK. Skip this delegate setup if JWT authentication isn’t needed. 

Zendesk.authenticationDelegate = AppAuthenticationDelegate { completion in
    Task {
        // Fetch a refreshed JWT from your backend.
        let refreshedJWT = await fetchFreshJWTFromBackend()
        completion(refreshedJWT)
    }
}
Zendesk.initialize(
    withChannelKey: "<channel_key>",
    messagingFactory: DefaultMessagingFactory()
) { result in
    if case let .failure(error) = result {
        // Handle initialization failure and run your app's fallback.
        print("Messaging did not initialize: \(error.localizedDescription)")
    }
}

Initialize the SDK when your app launches, and replace <channel_key> with the key for your messaging channel.

Your application should handle initialization failure explicitly.

Step 6: Configuring end-user authentication

Support SDK identities are not automatically transferred to the Messaging SDK.

  1. If your application authenticates end users, configure the supported messaging authentication flow using a Sunshine Conversations JWT. This remains required when users need access to restricted Help Center articles. The conversation-extension getContext token is a separate webview-to-backend authentication mechanism. Set up token refresh before initializing the SDK. 
    import ZendeskSDK

final class AppAuthenticationDelegate: AuthenticationDelegate {
    private let fetchToken: (@escaping (String) -> Void) -> Void

    init(fetchToken: @escaping (@escaping (String) -> Void) -> Void) {
        self.fetchToken = fetchToken
    }

    func onInvalidAuth(error: Error?, completion: @escaping (String) -> Void) {
        fetchToken(completion)
    }
}

Zendesk.authenticationDelegate = AppAuthenticationDelegate { completion in
    Task {
        // Fetch a fresh JWT from your backend.
        let refreshedJWT = await fetchFreshJWTFromBackend()
        completion(refreshedJWT)
    }
}
  2. Log in an authenticated user. After the SDK initializes, authenticate the user: 
    Zendesk.instance?.loginUser(with: jwt) { result in
    switch result {
    case .success(let user):
        // Authentication succeeded.
        break
    case .failure(let error):
        // Handle authentication failure.
        print("Authentication failed: \(error.localizedDescription)")
    }
}
  3. Replace fetchFreshJWTFromBackend() and jwt with your app’s backend token flow. The iOS authentication guide also documents logout and token-expiry behavior.

Step 7: Replacing Support SDK screens

For Android:

  1. Replace Support SDK entry points with the messaging conversation experience. Present the Messaging view controller where users open support: 
    if let viewController = Zendesk.instance?.messaging?.messagingViewController() {
    self.navigationController?.show(viewController, sender: self)
}

    By default, this opens the most recently active conversation.

  2. Remove or replace Support SDK screen entry points, including:
    • HelpCenterOverviewViewController
    • HelpCenterArticleViewController
    • RequestViewController
    • RequestListViewController
    • Answer Bot entry points
    Note: Before removing these entry points, confirm the approved replacement for each workflow. An AI agent can provide conversational article answers, but it does not replace standalone Help Center browsing and search. Use a Help Center webview or external browser for that workflow, and validate Messaging JWT authentication if restricted articles are required.

Step 8: Reconfiguring push notifications

The Support SDK push notification implementation does not apply to the Messaging SDK.

Do not reuse Support-specific Firebase services or configuration providers.

Follow the Messaging SDK push notification documentation to:

  • Register the device token with Zendesk.
  • Configure Apple Push Notification service for iOS.
  • Verify that a background message produces a notification.
  • Verify that selecting the notification opens the correct conversation.

Step 9: Cleaning up ProGuard and R8 rules

The Messaging SDK includes its consumer rules automatically.

  1. Remove obsolete Support SDK rules, such as: 
    -keepclassmembers class zendesk.support.** { *; }
-keep class zendesk.support.request.** { *; }
-keep class zendesk.support.requestlist.** { *; }
-keep class zendesk.support.request.ViewCellAttachmentMenuItem { *; }
  2. Review your project for other custom rules that reference removed Support SDK packages.

Step 10: Resolving build errors

  1. After replacing the Classic Support SDK with the Messaging SDK, build your app and update any remaining Support SDK dependencies and code references.
  2. For iOS, replace the Classic Support SDK imports with the Messaging SDK modules. Depending on your implementation, your existing imports may include SupportSDK, ZendeskCoreSDK, or SupportProvidersSDK. The Messaging SDK imports are ZendeskSDK and ZendeskSDKMessaging.
  3. Update any code that still references Support SDK screens, providers, or types to use the Messaging SDK APIs described in the steps above. Dependency names can vary by package manager, so follow the installation instructions for your chosen setup.

For Android iOS, the package roots change from:

Testing the migration in a sandbox

Test in a non-production Zendesk account using a dedicated messaging channel key.

Before releasing the migrated application, verify:

Build

  • The application builds successfully.
  • There are no unresolved Support SDK dependencies.
  • There are no conflicting Messaging SDK versions.

Initialization

  • The initialization success callback is called.
  • The failure callback is not called during normal startup.
  • The application handles initialization failure gracefully.

Messaging experience

  • The messaging entry point opens the conversation experience.
  • A message appears in Agent Workspace.
  • New conversations can be created successfully.
  • Attachments work as expected, if used.
  • Required forms, article workflows, and the approved Guide or Help Center replacement work as expected. If restricted articles are used, verify authenticated access with the Messaging JWT.

Authentication

  • An authenticated user can log in with a valid JWT.
  • The conversation is associated with the expected user.
  • An expired JWT triggers the token-refresh flow.
  • Logout returns the SDK to the visitor state.

Push notifications

  • A background message produces a notification.
  • Selecting the notification opens the relevant conversation.
  • Push behavior works on supported Android and iOS versions.

Rolling back the migration

The Support SDK and Messaging SDK use separate backends.

If you need to roll back before the migrated application is fully released:

  1. Revert the dependency changes.
  2. Restore Support SDK initialization.
  3. Restore Support SDK identity configuration.
  4. Restore Support SDK UI entry points.
  5. Restore Support SDK push notification configuration.
  6. Restore required Support SDK ProGuard or R8 rules.
  7. Rebuild and reinstall the application.

A rollback does not make messaging conversations visible in the Support SDK. Conversations created through messaging remain associated with the messaging channel and are not synchronized with the Support SDK backend.

Use staged rollout, feature flags, or an A/B testing mechanism where available to reduce deployment risk.

Releasing the migrated application

After sandbox testing is complete:

  1. Complete the required Zendesk account-side migration.
  2. Confirm that the required native SDK capabilities are production-ready.
  3. Merge the mobile code changes.
  4. Build the production application.
  5. Submit the application to the relevant app store.
  6. Use a staged rollout where available.
  7. Monitor initialization, authentication, messaging, push notifications, and crash reports.
  8. Confirm that end users are receiving the updated application.

The migration is complete only when affected end users have installed an application version that uses the Messaging SDK.

Older app versions may continue to exist after the new version is released.

Need help?

If you need help assessing your integration, contact your Zendesk account team or submit a support request through the standard Zendesk Support process.

articles.name: Replacing legacy ticket creation workflows with AI agent tickets
articles.title: Replacing legacy ticket creation workflows with AI agent tickets
articles.body:
TheAI agent ticketsfeature automatically creates a ticket at the start of every AI agent conversation. That ticket is used to keep all context, outcomes, and reporting about the conversation in one place.

What's my plan?
All Suites Team, Growth, Professional, Enterprise, or Enterprise Plus
Support Team, Professional, or Enterprise

The AI agent tickets feature automatically creates a ticket at the start of every AI agent conversation. That ticket is used to keep all context, outcomes, and reporting about the conversation in one place.

Prior to the introduction of the AI agent tickets feature, there was no standard way to create a ticket for an AI agent conversation. As a workaround, you may have previously set up one or more or the following workflows to create a ticket to record an AI agent conversation:

  • A configured action using the Create ticket action
  • An API integration using the Create Ticket API
  • The “Send an email” option of an Escalation block in a dialogue

These workflows were often configured to run when an AI agent conversation ended, and either created or updated a ticket in order to:

  • Escalate AI agent conversations as tickets instead of messaging conversations
  • Log AI agent conversations for reporting
  • Set ticket fields via an action or API payload

With the introduction of AI agent tickets, these workflows are considered legacy and will result in duplicate tickets if they run after the AI agent tickets feature is turned on in your account:

  • Ticket 1: Created automatically by the AI agent tickets feature when the AI agent conversation starts.
  • Ticket 2: Created by your legacy workflow at either the end of the conversation or during escalation.

The result is two tickets for one customer issue, leading to split context, a confusing agent experience, and inconsistent reporting. To eliminate the possibility of duplicate tickets, update any legacy ticket creation workflows you previously created as part of your escalation flows.

This article contains the following topics:

  • Before you start: A note about asynchronous ticket escalations
  • Identifying legacy ticket creation workflows
  • Updating escalation flows that use the Create ticket action
  • Updating escalation flows that use an API integration
  • Updating escalation flows that use the “Send an email” option
  • Testing your updates

Before you start: A note about asynchronous ticket escalations

Escalation flows can be either real-time, meaning customers are immediately transferred from your AI agent to a human agent, or asynchronous, meaning customers can leave messages when a human agent is unavailable. Regardless of whether your escalation flows are real-time or asynchronous, you need to follow the guidance in this article to update any legacy ticket creation workflows.

However, if you’ve configured asynchronous escalations, you should also follow the steps in Workflow recipe: Configuring asynchronous ticket escalations for messaging AI agents.

The goal with asynchronous escalations is to have one ticket for each AI agent conversation, while ensuring out-of-hours requests don’t sit in a live messaging queue or skew live-chat metrics. This applies to any availability-based escalation where live messaging is unavailable, undesirable, or an asynchronous Zendesk ticket is preferred.

Identifying legacy ticket creation workflows

As you get started with identifying any legacy ticket creation workflows, you may find it useful to create a spreadsheet to track your updates. Start by listing all of your AI agents, visible on the dashboard in the AI agents workspace. For each AI agent, record its associated escalation-related configuration, discussed below.

First, check whether you’ve created a configured action or API integration that creates a ticket. These configured actions and API integrations can be reused across dialogues. To review your:

  • Configured actions:
    1. In the AI agents workspace, select the AI agent you want to work with.
    2. Click Actions in the sidebar, then select Configured actions.
    3. Click each configured action to open its details to see whether it contains the Create ticket action.
    4. If it does, note this configured action in your tracking spreadsheet.
  • API integrations:
    1. In the AI agents workspace, select the AI agent you want to work with.
    2. Click Actions in the sidebar, then select API integrations.
    3. Click each API integration to open its details and see whether it uses the Create Ticket API.
    4. If it does, note this API integration in your tracking spreadsheet.

Next, identify all escalation flows you may have configured in your AI agent. Escalation flows can be configured as part of the Escalation reply system reply, dialogues, or templates. To review your:

  • Escalation reply:
    1. In the AI agents workspace, select the AI agent you want to work with.
    2. Click Content in the sidebar, then select Use cases.
    3. Click the Categories filter, select System replies, and click Apply.
    4. Find the one called Escalation reply and review its associated dialogue to look for:
      • Any configured actions you noted above that use the Create ticket action
      • Any API integrations you noted above that use the Create Ticket API
      • An Escalation block with the “Send an email” option
    5. Note your findings in your tracking spreadsheet.
  • Dialogues:
    1. In the AI agents workspace, select the AI agent you want to work with.
    2. Click Content in the sidebar, then select Use cases.
    3. For any use case that has a Reply method of Dialogue, open the associated dialogue and look for:
      • Any configured actions you noted above that use the Create ticket action
      • Any API integrations you noted above that use the Create Ticket API
      • An Escalation block with the “Send an email” option
    4. For any dialogues that contain any of the above, note your findings in your tracking spreadsheet.
  • Templates:
    1. In the AI agents workspace, select the AI agent you want to work with.
    2. Click Content in the sidebar, then select Templates.
    3. For each template, open its associated dialogue in the Replies column and look for:
      • Any configured actions you noted above that use the Create ticket action
      • An API integrations you noted above that use the Create Ticket API
      • An Escalation block with the “Send an email” option
    4. For any templates that contain any of the above, note your findings in your tracking spreadsheet.

At this point, review your tracking spreadsheet and answer the following questions for each of the escalation flows you recorded:

  • Does this escalation flow use the Create ticket action?
    • Yes: See Updating escalation flows that use the Create ticket action.
    • No: Continue reading.
  • Does this escalation flow use an API integration that creates Zendesk tickets?
    • Yes: See Updating escalation flows that use an API integration.
    • No: Continue reading.
  • Does this escalation flow use the “Send an email” option in an Escalation in a dialogue?
    • Yes: See Updating escalation flows that use the “Send an email” option.
    • No: If you don’t use any of the legacy ticket creation workflows listed above and you still see duplicate tickets for AI agent conversations, you may have a custom setup (for example, triggers or external workflows creating tickets). Contact Zendesk customer support for further assistance.

Updating escalation flows that use the Create ticket action

If any of your escalation flows include a configured action that uses the Create ticket action, update or remove this configured action, as it’s no longer necessary with the AI agent tickets feature.

This section also applies to AI agent–level actions that are executed in every conversation your AI agent engages in, even if they’re not specifically added in a dialogue.

To update escalation flows that use the Create ticket action

  1. In the AI agents workspace, select the AI agent you want to work with.
  2. Click Actions in the sidebar, then select Configured actions.
  3. Find the configured action that uses the Create ticket action and do either of the following:
    • If the configured action includes other actions besides Create ticket (such as adding tags, custom fields, or routing information), edit it to remove the Create ticket action while leaving the other actions.
      Tip: If these actions should be applied to every escalation, make sure you’re using an AI agent–level action.
    • If the configured action includes only the Create ticket action, delete it.
  4. Test your updates.

Updating escalation flows that use an API integration

If any of your escalation flows include an API integration that uses the Create Ticket API, update or remove this API integration, as it’s no longer necessary with the AI agent tickets feature.

Note that there is an exception to this guidance: You may still need the API integration if you’re creating tickets in another Zendesk instance (cross-instance routing).

To update escalation flows that use an API integration

  1. In the AI agents workspace, select the AI agent you want to work with.
  2. Click Actions in the sidebar, then select API integrations.
  3. Find the API integration that uses the Create Ticket API and open it for editing.
  4. (Optional) If the API integration includes other actions besides creating a ticket, such as passing fields or tags information, create and add a configured action to pass that information instead.
    Tip: If these actions should be applied to every escalation, make sure you’re using an AI agent–level action.
  5. Delete the API integration.
  6. Test your updates.

Updating escalation flows that use the “Send an email” option

If any of your escalation flows include an Escalation block with the “Send an email” option, update the option to “Forward to agent” instead.

To update escalation flows that use the “Send an email” option

  1. Open a dialogue that includes an Escalation block that uses the “Send an email” option.
  2. In the Escalation block, click Send an email and select Forward to an agent instead.
  3. (Optional) If the goal of your original configuration was to notify another team or external party, also use action flows, side conversations, or a similar workflow automation to handle the notification.
  4. Test your updates.

Testing your updates

After making your updates, test the end-to-end customer experience to ensure the conversational experience, ticket routing, and reporting all work as expected. For help, see the following testing resources:

  • Testing conversation flows in AI agents
  • Best practices for testing AI agents

Additionally, make sure you understand the AI agent ticket experience so you know what the expected behavior is:

  • Understanding AI agent tickets for AI agent–only conversations
  • Finding AI agent tickets in your account
  • Interacting with AI agent tickets

As part of your tests, make sure you include the following:

  • AI agent conversations that resolve without escalation. You should see one AI agent ticket, and it should have a status of Solved.
    Note: Previously, the legacy ticket creation workflows may have assigned the tickets to a group, even for AI agent–resolved conversations. With AI agent tickets, AI agent–resolved tickets aren’t assigned to anyone, because no handoff occurred. This is expected behavior.
  • AI agent conversations that result in escalation. You should see one editable ticket that a human agent can work.

In both scenarios, validate that the ticket contains any updated fields or tags added by your configured actions, if applicable.

articles.name: Why do my SMS messages fail to send?
articles.title: Why do my SMS messages fail to send?
articles.body:
Question

Scenario A

I receive one of the error messages below when I send an outbound Text message:

  • We couldn't deliver this message
  • We couldn't send the message
Scenario B

When I review the message details in my Text history, the status of my message is either Undelivered or Failed:

Why are my SMS messages failing?

Answer

Multiple reasons exist for SMS message failure. Common reasons why SMS messages fail to send:

  • The destination handset is unreachable.
  • The destination phone number doesn't support text.
  • The end user sent an opt-out code to one of my messages. For more information on opt-outs, see About opt-out keywords for Zendesk Text.
  • The destination number isn't local and international texting hasn't been enabled. Contact Zendesk Customer Support if you want to enable international texting.
  • The destination number is located in a country where the text number doesn't support SMS long code international messaging. For example, Zendesk US text numbers can't send SMS messages to UK numbers. For more information, see Twilio's SMS guidelines.

If SMS messages still fail to send or if you need your US/CA toll-free numbers verified, contact Zendesk Customer Support with the ticket ID where the SMS message failed for further assistance.

articles.name: Configuring call console access in Contact Center
articles.title: Configuring call console access in Contact Center
articles.body:
Admins can control which team members can use the Contact Center call console. The call console icon () doesn’t display in the workspace of a team member who doesn’t have access.

What's my plan?
Add-on Contact Center

Summary: ◀▼

You can control who sees the call console by limiting access with roles and groups. Team members need at least one matching role and one matching group to use it, while empty lists don’t restrict access. This helps you manage call console access, user permissions, and call routing for the right support team members.

Location: Contact Center > Overview

Admins can control which team members can use the Contact Center call console. The call console icon () doesn’t display in the workspace of a team member who doesn’t have access.

You can restrict call console access to the team members who need it by selecting the Zendesk roles and groups they must belong to. By default, no roles or groups are selected, giving all team members access to the call console.

Team members must have at least one selected role and belong to at least one selected group to access the call console. If you leave either list empty, that list doesn’t limit access.

Note: Amazon Connect admins must also assign the team members a security profile with access to the Amazon Connect Contact Control Panel. For more information, see Provide agents with access to the Connect Customer Contact Control Panel (CCP) in Amazon documentation.

To configure call console access

  1. In Contact Center, click Overview.

    The console access configuration is under Call console access.

  2. Click the Roles menu, then select the roles that can have access to the call console.

    To help find roles, you can search the list by role name. Matching roles appear as you type.

    By default, no role is selected, meaning roles don't limit access.

    When you select roles, a team member must have at least one of the selected roles to access the call console.

  3. Click the Groups menu, then select the groups that can have access to the call console.

    To help find groups, you can search the list by group name. Matching groups appear as you type.

    By default, no group is selected, meaning group membership doesn't limit access.

    When you select groups, a team member must belong to at least one of the selected groups to access the call console.

  4. Click Save.

Now that you've given team members access to the console, let them know that they need to configure their browser for calls.

articles.name: Can the WhatsApp "Message Us" button label be translated into multiple languages?
articles.title: Can the WhatsApp "Message Us" button label be translated into multiple languages?
articles.body:
Question

Can I translate the WhatsApp Message Us button into multiple languages in Zendesk?

Answer

The Message Us button is configured in Zendesk > Admin Center > Channels > Messaging and Social > Messaging. That button currently supports only a single Label field. There is no built-in option to set different label translations per language within that configuration.

To make the button language-aware, replace the hardcoded text with a Zendesk Dynamic Content placeholder. Dynamic content automatically displays the correct language variant based on the end user's detected locale.

Step 1: Create the Dynamic Content Item

  1. In Admin Center, click Workspaces in the sidebar.
  2. Select Agent tools > Dynamic content.
  3. Click Add item.
  4. Enter a descriptive title (e.g., message_us_button_label).
  5. Select your default language and enter the default button label text.
  6. Click Create.

Step 2: Add Language Variants

  1. Open the dynamic content item you just created.
  2. Click Add variant to create versions for each of your supported languages.
  3. Select the target language and enter the translated label text.
  4. Set the variant status to either Active that will display to users viewing the Help Center in that language, or Inactive and users in that language will see the default language variant instead.
  5. Save your changes and copy the generated placeholder code.

Step 3: Update Your HTML Snippet

In the HTML code, replace the hardcoded label value in your iframe snippet with your dynamic content placeholder.

Example snippet: label={{dc 'name_of_your_dynamic_content_with_underscores' }}

Important considerations

  • Fallback language: If an end user's language is not supported or active in your Dynamic Content settings, the system automatically displays your designated default variant.
  • Locale matching: Ensure the language code selected in your dynamic content variant matches the exact locale enabled under Admin Center > Account > Appearance > Languages (for example, English (US) vs. English (UK)).

articles.name: Troubleshooting issues in the new article editor
articles.title: Troubleshooting issues in the new article editor
articles.body:
When you move to the new article editor from the legacy editor, you might notice changes to tables, links, spacing, lists, or headings. Use the sections below to find the issue and try the relevant fix.

Before changing your help center theme or article source code, back up the content or CSS you plan to edit. Preview changes before publishing.

Troubleshooting issues with tables

How to fix a table wrap in <figure> elements

The new article editor uses <figure> tags to provide consistent styles and features for tables across different browsers and platforms. This behavior is part of the new editor's table plugin architecture. It can cause style issues, such as a restricted table height or unwanted format issues. This section explains why this happens and how to prevent or fix it.

Important: Back up your CSS and content before you make major changes.

The new article editor wraps tables in <figure class="table"> elements and may apply inline styles that override custom classes.

To restore your table styles:

  1. Update your CSS selectors to target the new markup:
    • figure.table table { /* your table styles */ }
    • figure.table th, figure.table td { /* cell styles */ }
  2. Use !important sparingly to override inline styles if needed
  3. Test your changes in a duplicate article before you apply them site-wide

To prevent or fix table wrap issues:

  • Review your help center CSS to ensure that <figure class="table"> elements don't have restrictive styles, such as max-height or overflow settings
  • If you see style issues, update your CSS to target <figure class="table"> as shown:
    figure.table {
    max-height: none;
    overflow: visible;
    }
  • If you migrate content, don't remove <figure> tags by hand. The new article editor may add them again when you edit content.
Note: This guidance is based on general product knowledge and is not explicitly present in the original tickets. The new article editor relies on <figure> wrappers by design for feature support and consistency. Use help center CSS customization to resolve style issues, not changes to the editor output HTML.

How to fix table header and header level format issues

Common format issues after migration:

  • Table headers may lose their background color or styles
  • Table header cells may convert incorrectly to H2 text
  • H2, H3 sizes may appear different due to changes in default or custom CSS
  • The editor may not save table changes as expected

To ensure that table headers display correctly after migration:

  1. In your help center theme, add CSS rules that target <thead> or <th> elements, for example:
    thead { background-color: #f5f5f5; }
    th { background-color: #f5f5f5; }
  2. Keep or update any existing <th> styles to maintain consistency

To set table headers in the new article editor:

  1. In the article, select your table, then click the top row
  2. From the Row dropdown, turn on the Header row option
    • If the header row option is missing, manually add <thead> and <th> elements in the HTML source, or check for available plugins or editor options in your new article editor setup

If H2 or H3 styles appear incorrect

Review and update header levels:

  1. Edit the article in the new article editor
  2. Select any table header text that the editor converted to H2
  3. Change its format to the correct style, such as a table header or normal text

Adjust header level sizes with CSS:

  1. Go to Knowledge admin > Customize design > Customize > Edit code > style.css
  2. Update the CSS to ensure that H2, H3, and similar styles match your desired sizes
  3. Use the Preview feature to check the final format before you click Publish

If the editor doesn't save your table changes or you see errors like no changes have been made:

  1. Try to reproduce the issue
  2. Capture an HTTP Archive (HAR) file and a screen capture
  3. Contact Zendesk Customer Support for further help

See

  • Fixing table styling when transitioning to the new article editor
  • Adding and formatting tables in help center articles
Tip: If you have many articles to update, consider a batch script or a migration tool to standardize header levels and styles, and back up your articles every time before you make bulk changes. If your new article editor implementation lacks certain table features, check for available plugins or contact your platform admin for enhancements.

How to fix table format and alignment issues

Common issues after migration:

  • Custom table styles for width and borders do not apply as before
  • Inconsistent text size and cell space
  • Table classes and border styles changed during a migration
  • Header rows split between <thead> and <tbody>, which causes style inconsistencies
  • Text overflow and table border issues

To fix these issues:

  • Update your help center CSS to target table elements
    .article-body td, .article-body th {
    padding: 20px;
    font-size: 16px;
    }
  • Fix table alignment
    • Use the new article editor table alignment options. The new article editor may have fewer features than the legacy editor.
    • If tables center every time or alignment does not work, add or adjust CSS:
      .article-body table {
      margin-left: 0 !important;
      margin-right: auto !important;
      }
  • Manage table cell space and alignment
    • Remove unnecessary inline styles that set cell space so your theme CSS controls that property
    • Define the desired cell space in your theme CSS
  • Adjust table classes, borders, and headers
    • Update CSS rules for any new or changed table classes, for example, .nonItemList
    • Ensure that all header rows are inside <thead> for proper styling
    • Move any header rows from <tbody> to <thead> as needed
  • Table text escapes borders or does not wrap as expected, especially after you add a table border in the article editor
    • Use these help center theme CSS rules to ensure table cell text wracts correctly and stays within the table borders
      /* 1. Target the class name from your table tag */
      table.wysiwyg-table-resized {
      /* This tells the browser: "Do not look at the content to decide width.
      Look at the <col> widths (40%/60%) and obey them strictly." */
      table-layout: fixed;
      width: 100%;
      }

      /* 2. Target the cells to ensure wrapping happens */
      table.wysiwyg-table-resized td {
      /* Forces text to go to the next line when it hits the edge */
      white-space: normal;

      /* Breaks long words/URLs if they are too wide for the 60% column */
      overflow-wrap: break-word;
      word-wrap: break-word;

      /* Optional: Makes reading easier by aligning text to the top */
      vertical-align: top;
      }
  • Articles edited or migrated from earlier versions of Zendesk Guide may contain legacy formatting that conflicts with your current theme CSS. If fixes do not apply as expected, inspect the table’s HTML and remove extra formatting or attributes that may affect layout.
    • In the article editor, select the table and remove any specific width or style settings applied through the article editor table controls
    • If necessary, switch to the HTML view and delete width attributes or inline style tags from <table>, <tr>, or <td> elements
  • Test and verify changes
    • Preview affected articles in the new article editor to confirm the formatting
    • Repeat for each article with custom tables, as a manual review may be required

Troubleshooting issues with links

Immediate workarounds

If you see these issues, switch to the legacy editor.

To do this:

  1. In the Article settings panel, select Switch to legacy editor
  2. Update the hyperlink in the legacy editor
  3. Switch back to the new article editor
  4. When you switch editors, use the feedback prompt to report the issue to the engineering team

If the visual editor does not update links, edit them in HTML:

  1. Open the article in the new article editor
  2. Click the Source code icon on the toolbar
  3. Locate the <a> tag, the anchor for the link you need to edit
  4. Update the URL or link text
  5. To open the link in a new tab, add target="_blank" rel="noopener" to the <a> tag.
    For example: <a href="URL" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Link Text</a>
  6. Save your changes and switch back to the visual editor to confirm the link appears and works as expected

More fixes

  • Update the article editor to the latest version. Check for patches.
  • After you update, clear your browser cache to load the latest editor
  • Edit and insert links to check if the issues are fixed
  • If problems continue, contact your support team or product manager. Include your browser version and steps to show the issue.
  • If you are not sure a fix is live, ask your support contact or check platform announcements
  • If problems remain after updates, clear your cache again or use a different browser to check for browser or cache issues

Troubleshooting formatting issues

Extra spaces and line breaks

To fix this:

  1. Review your articles for extra spaces or blank lines, especially between paragraphs, lists, and headings
  2. Open the article in the new article editor
  3. Click the Source code icon from the toolbar
  4. Remove unnecessary <br> tags or extra spaces, especially inside lists or near headings
  5. Save and preview the article to confirm the issue is resolved

Bullet lists <ul> display as numbered lists

Reason: Your theme CSS overrides the default style.

To fix this:

  1. Go to Knowledge admin > Customize design > Customize > Edit code > style.CSS
  2. Inspect your CSS for rules such as ul { list-style-type: decimal; }
  3. Change or add ul { list-style-type: disc; }
  4. Use the Preview feature to check the final format before you click Publish

Nested and multi-level don’t display correctly

Reason: The new article editor doesn’t natively support mixed-style nested lists. For example, numbers for the first level and letters for the second, in the editor UI.

To fix this, update your theme CSS to create custom nested number styles in published articles.

Add CSS such as:

ol {
    counter-reset: item;
    padding-left: 10px;
  }
  li {
    display: block;
  }
  li:before {
    content: counters(item, ".") " ";
    counter-increment: item;
  }
Tip: Use the Preview feature every time to check the final format before you save and publish.

In the editor, nested lists might show a uniform number style, but the published view restores the correct hierarchy (numbers, letters, Roman numerals). A custom number style might not appear in the editor preview unless you insert CSS in the article source, which isn't recommended for maintenance reasons.

Heading formats go missing or reset after you press Enter

To fix this:

  1. Open the article in the new article editor
  2. Refresh your browser and clear the cache
  3. Contact Zendesk Customer Support for further help.

articles.name: Why doesn't a solved ticket appear in real-time monitoring charts where I expect?
articles.title: Why doesn't a solved ticket appear in real-time monitoring charts where I expect?
articles.body:
Question

I solved or updated a ticket, but why isn't it showing up in the time period I expect on a real-time monitoring report?

Answer

Some real-time charts group ticket activity by when a ticket enters a specific state. For example, charts track when a user creates a ticket or when it enters a queue, rather than when you update or solve it.

An earlier event, rather than the most recent update, generally locks in a ticket's position on the chart. If you solve a ticket today, it doesn't necessarily move into today's bucket on every chart. The chart may measure a different moment in the ticket lifecycle.

A few examples of how this works:

  • Queue activity charts, for example, Standard queue activity for email, track when a ticket entered or exited a specific queue. Solving the ticket later doesn't change when it entered or exited that queue, so it remains in that original time window.
  • Ticket-count and satisfaction charts that use rolling time buckets assign each ticket to the bucket active during ticket creation. They don't assign tickets based on when you update, solve, or rate them. If you solve an older ticket today, the chart still links it to its original creation bucket. The ticket might not appear in a shorter time window that only looks back a few days.
  • Because the system recalculates bucket boundaries every time the dashboard loads, they don't match the ticket creation time. The same ticket can appear in a different bucket on a later view, even when nothing about the ticket changed. For example, an August 16 ticket might appear in the August 15 bucket if the nearest boundary fell at 9:04:55 PM on August 15. This occurs if someone creates the ticket just before the next boundary at 9:04:55 PM on August 16.
  • In some cases, the system finalizes the chart's underlying record after a specific field, such as an end time, receives a value. If that happens before a later status change, the chart won't retroactively reflect that later change.

What this means for you

This is expected behavior, not missing or broken data. The ticket data itself remains intact. However, the chart measures a specific moment in time rather than the most recent update, and bucket boundaries can shift between views.

To confirm a ticket's current status or historical changes, check the ticket itself. You can also report on it using a standard Zendesk Analytics dataset, such as Tickets or Updates history.

Use real-time monitoring charts to track current workload and activity trends, rather than as an audit trail of every status change.

articles.name: Why do real-time monitoring charts show a time or date that hasn't happened yet?
articles.title: Why do real-time monitoring charts show a time or date that hasn't happened yet?
articles.body:
Question

Why do real-time monitoring charts show a time or date that hasn't happened yet?

Answer

This is expected behavior. Real-time monitoring charts don't group data into fixed clock-hour or calendar-day buckets the way a standard historical report does. Instead, they build their time buckets backward from the exact moment you open the dashboard. They set the edge of the most recent bucket to the next upcoming boundary every time, rather than the last one that passed.

This design means the chart's current bucket includes active tickets and tickets with recent updates. The chart does not wait for a boundary to close fully before showing that activity.

The system calculates bucket boundaries in UTC and displays them in your account's local time zone. The label on that final bar can look like it's ahead of "now," especially if your time zone is several hours ahead of UTC.

How the time buckets work

The size of each bucket depends on the reporting window you select:

  • Last 15–120 minutes: 5–30 minutes
  • Last 8–24 hours: 1–3 hours
  • Last 48 hours: 6 hours
  • Last 7 or 14 days: 1 day
  • Last 30 days: 1 day

The system rounds up each bucket boundary to the next clean UTC interval for that bucket size. For an hourly chart, boundaries land on even UTC hours, such as 00:00, 03:00, and 06:00 UTC. For a daily chart, every boundary lands on UTC midnight.

Example: hourly chart that shows a future time

With a 24-hour reporting window, buckets are 3 hours apart and align with UTC. For example, if you view the dashboard at 11:54 AM in a time zone that's UTC+11, that's 12:54 AM UTC. The next 3-hour UTC boundary is 3:00 AM UTC, which displays in your local time zone as 2:00 PM. The latest bar shows this time.

Example: daily chart that shows tomorrow's date

With a 7-day reporting window, buckets are 1 day apart and align with UTC midnight. If you view the dashboard at 12:08 PM 08/10/2026 in a time zone that's UTC+11, that's 1:08 AM UTC. The next UTC midnight is tomorrow at 12:00 AM UTC, which displays in your local time zone as 11:00 AM 09/10/2026 tomorrow's date. The latest bar shows this date.

Does this mean my data is wrong?

No. The ticket counts in each bar are accurate for the window of time that bucket represents. Only the label on the bucket boundary changes. The system recalculates the boundary relative to the moment you load the dashboard, rather than fixing it to your local clock.

If you reload the dashboard, the bucket boundaries shift forward again to match the refreshed time, and the labels update accordingly.

articles.body:

To appear in the changelog, a change must have passed validation (for example, all mandatory field conditions are met) and have been successfully saved to the system without encountering errors.

Viewing the changelog for an AI agent

You can view the changelog for an AI agent from the AI agents workspace.

To view the changelog for an AI agent

  1. In the AI agents workspace, select the AI agent you want to work with.
  2. Click Optimize in the sidebar, then select Monitoring > Changelog.

    The Change log page opens, with each tracked event represented as a row in the table.

  3. Review the information in the following columns:

    • Last update: Date and time of the change

    • Action: Specifics of the change

    • User: Who made the change

  4. If necessary, use the page navigation at the bottom to move to the next page of results.

    Tip: You can modify how many rows appear on each page using the Row dropdown.

A change appears only if it passed validation, such as meeting all mandatory field conditions, and was successfully saved without errors.

articles.name: Every incoming email sent to my Zendesk is suspended
articles.title: Every incoming email sent to my Zendesk is suspended
articles.body:
Issue symptoms

I set up email forwarding from an external support address to my Zendesk and now every email appears on the suspended view.

Causes

The cause of these suspended emails usually is an incorrect set of a web form with email forwarding, a spammy sender, or an issue with email headers and automations. For more information, see Causes for ticket suspension.

Additional suspension causes include:

  • Received from support address indicates that your email server is configured with an external support address, for example, support@example.com, as the From or Reply-To header in every email forwarded to your Zendesk. These messages are suspended by Zendesk due to the ability to cause mail loops. To resolve this issue, modify the email forwarding on your server to show the email address of the ticket requester email address rather than your external support address in the From or Reply-To header.
  • Automated response email indicates that the email server is adding an automated header such as Precedence: bulk or Auto-submitted: auto-generated to every email that is forwarded to your Zendesk account. These headers tell Zendesk that the messages were auto-generated rather than created by end users. To resolve this issue, modify the email forwarding on your server to not add either of these headers to forwarded email messages.

Resolution steps

To avoid all emails being suspended or rejected, follow these steps:

  1. Verify if you use a web form with email. This isn't supported and causes errors. Instead, use the API to generate tickets from forms.
  2. Ensure that your support address doesn't use unsupported aliases or email groups. Instead, use a regular email address.
  3. Ensure that forwarding is set up at the server level, instead of in the individual settings of your email address.
  4. Verify your SPF record.
  5. The email header cannot contain unsupported entries under Automated response from Causes for ticket suspension. For example, Delivered-To, Auto-Submitted, or Autoresponder are not supported.
  6. Don't use an email address that starts with noreply@, daemon@, or postmaster@, as these are not supported.
  7. Verify that the emails do not contain any unsubscribe links, as these are not supported.
  8. Verify that the emails are not automatic replies, as these are not supported.
  9. If after verifying the above, you are still facing issues, further troubleshooting is required. Take a full page screenshot of one example (including the sender, receiver, and time) and share it with Zendesk Customer Support.
Note: If you don't have access to your email server, reach out to your email administrator or email hosting company. Modify your email forwarding in order to resolve issues.
